scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El músico de heavy sale del público: es el fan que toca la guitarra de aire en el concierto de UFO de 1979 y quiere estar donde está Michael Schenker. No hay escuela ni beca: hace falta talento musical y dramático (actuar la emoción por trescientas veces), un cuerpo joven y atlético (correr y pesas en la gira, el pelo largo como signo de autenticidad) y aprender a vivir en un grupo que no es ni familia ni oficina, con sus «problemas de ego» por la rivalidad entre cantante y guitarrista. El heavy es el estilo más caro de montar y casi no hay clubes donde empezar; el código exige temas propios y autenticidad. Firmar con un sello convierte a la banda en una empresa del capitalismo tardío frente a un oligopolio. El ciclo es componer, grabar (paciencia; el primer disco de Black Sabbath se hizo en doce horas, Spreading the Disease de Anthrax en cinco meses) y girar (aguante: esperar, esperar). La recompensa no es el dinero sino el carisma del chamán que alcanza el éxtasis dionisíaco ante miles de personas; el precio, «quemarse o apagarse», porque nadie que viva lo bastante puede cumplir el código.

podcast.title: Metallica's Lawsuit Against Napster – Legal Action and Public Stance
podcast.body: In the spring of 2000, Metallica discovered unreleased band files on Napster. This prompted them to sue Napster in April 2000. To emphasize their point, a dramatic photo opportunity was staged where a list of approximately 350,000 Napster users trading Metallica files, comprising 60,000 pages and documenting 1.4 million copyright violations of 95 Metallica songs, was delivered in front of television cameras. The band declared their intention to pursue legal action against downloaders. "Our team of lawyers and researchers have your names And we're going to hunt you down like a table scrap pilfering grab as you are."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opposition to Music Downloading – Leading the Charge Against Napster
podcast.body: Lars Ulrich's most significant impact beyond his musical contributions has been his vigorous opposition to music downloading. He was the public face and the driving force behind the mission to shut down the original Napster, arguing that free music downloading directly takes money from the pockets of musicians and the creative community, whose primary income source is record sales. "Lars was the guy who made an emission to shut down the original Napster For better or worse, he was the guy the public face who led the charge against anyone who downloaded music for free."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cliff Burton's Death (1986)
xref.body: Former Metallica bassist Cliff Burton died in a tour bus accident in 1986. His initials (CBL) and a transcription of his song "Orion" are tattooed on James Hetfield as a tribute. "That's a transcription of the song Orion, which is in tribute to former Metallica bass player Cliff Burton, who died in a tour bus accident in 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lawsuit Against Napster (2000)
xref.body: Metallica, notably with drummer Lars Ulrich as the public face, filed a lawsuit against Napster on April 30, 2000, after discovering their unreleased demo "I Disappear" and their entire catalog were being freely traded online. Lars Ulrich physically delivered a 60,000-page list of 335,435 alleged Metallica song pirates to Napster's offices. The band sought at least $10 million in damages, a ban for all users trading Metallica songs, and university crackdowns on student downloading. This action generated intense fan backlash, damaging Metallica's reputation as "rich rock stars, bullying fans." Despite this, Napster was ultimately shut down in July 2001 after settling with Metallica and Dr. Dre, confirming that its practices violated copyright. "On April 30, 2000, they made a big deal of launching a lawsuit with drummer Lars Alrich becoming the face of the proceedings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Until It Sleeps" Web Cartoon
xref.body: A popular web cartoon satirized Lars Ulrich's stance against Napster users, depicting him as ungrateful and threatening to fans who downloaded their music. "Like, good afternoon. My name is Lars Ulrich from Metallica... Unless you downloaded until it sleeps from Napster, then you're going to m**king jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Continued Bad Blood with Dave Mustaine
xref.body: Despite both bands achieving success, a sense of lingering tension between Metallica and Dave Mustaine, particularly with Lars Ulrich, persisted for a long time. The 2004 Metallica documentary "Some Kind of Monster" shows a confrontation between Dave Mustaine and Lars Ulrich where nothing was resolved, and back-and-forth public comments continued for another decade. While many issues have since been resolved, the impression of underlying tension remains. "If you watch the 2004 Metallica documentary, some kind of monster, you can see a confrontation between Dave and drummer Lars Altrek."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Continued Bad Blood with Metallica
xref.body: Despite Megadeth's success, a lasting tension between Dave Mustaine and Metallica, particularly Lars Ulrich, has been noted. A confrontation between Mustaine and Ulrich was depicted in the 2004 Metallica documentary "Some Kind of Monster," and public disputes continued for a decade afterward, with underlying tension often felt to remain. "And somehow I still get the impression that there's some bad blood there. If you watch the 2004 Metallica documentary, some kind of monster, you can see a confrontation between Dave and drummer Lars Altrek."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lars Ulrich's Congressional Testimony
xref.body: Lars Ulrich testified in Washington, D.C., about the "evils of piracy, file sharing, and copyright infringement," expanding the debate beyond music to general information exchange. "Lars ended up testifying in Washington about the evils of piracy, file sharing, and copyright infringement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lars Ulrich's Napster Office Visit
xref.body: Lars Ulrich delivered a 60,000-page printout listing 335,435 Napster users who allegedly poached Metallica songs to the Napster offices, generating significant media attention. "Then, with great media fanfare, Lars Ulrich pulled up in front of the Napster offices, in Olimom, with a 60,000-page printout of 335,435 Napster users, who allegedly had poached Metallica songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Son of Lars Ulrich
xref.body: Miles Ulrich is one of Lars Ulrich's sons and plays drums for the band Taipei Houston. "Miles is the drummer and Lane, whose three years younger sings in place bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Son of Lars Ulrich
xref.body: Layne Ulrich is one of Lars Ulrich's sons, three years younger than Miles, and performs vocals and plays bass for Taipei Houston. "Miles is the drummer and Lane, whose three years younger sings in place bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Viral "Eleanor Rigby" Cover
xref.body: Taipei Houston initially gained notoriety when Lars Ulrich, the father of two band members, posted a video clip of them performing a hard and heavy version of The Beatles' "Eleanor Rigby." "They first found some notoriety when dad posted a clip of them doing a hard and heavy version of the Beatles Eleanor Rigby."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
